title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a bell is struck and fades, and a Nyaya teacher turns that fading into an argument in five steps

segments.voice: This week began with the long night of Maha Shivaratri, then turned to the six darshanas, schools of thought never ranked. Yesterday brought Nyaya, logic. Today closes the week.
screen: `FROM SHIVA'S NIGHT TO THE SIX SCHOOLS.` · `NYAYA, CONTINUED.`

segments.voice: Somebody strikes a bell. The note blooms out into the room, hangs there, thins, and then it's gone. Nobody is surprised. Of course it faded. But a teacher of Nyaya would stop you right there: how do you know it had to fade? You heard this one bell, not every sound there will ever be. Nyaya takes that small, ordinary leap and slows it down until you can see every step. Today, one of its tools: an argument in five parts, said out loud, so the other person can check each one.
screen: `A BELL, AND THEN SILENCE.` → `HOW DO YOU KNOW IT HAD TO FADE?` → `AN ARGUMENT IN FIVE PARTS.`

segments.voice: The Nyaya Sutra names the five parts: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. Its early commentator, Vatsyayana, walks them through with sound itself. One: sound does not last. Two: because it is produced. Three: whatever is produced does not last, like a clay pot. Four: sound, too, is produced. Five: so sound does not last. It sounds slow, even a little silly. But look at step three, because that's where the whole thing lives. It names the rule out loud, then points to a case both people have seen with their own eyes. Pots get made, and pots break. An argument in Nyaya isn't one mind talking to itself. It's two people looking at the same pot. If you can't point to a shared case where your rule plainly holds, the argument doesn't stand. And because the rule is said out loud, the other person can test it. Not everyone agreed with this one. Thinkers of the Mimamsa school held that the sounds of the Veda are eternal, and they argued the point with Nyaya. Nyaya's answer wasn't to shout louder. It was to lay out the steps, so the disagreement could land on the step where it really lived. Now bring it home. A friend doesn't text back. One: they're upset with me. Two: because they haven't answered. Three: whoever doesn't answer is upset, like… and there you stop. Where's your pot?
screen: `FIVE PARTS, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `SOUND DOESN'T LAST, LIKE A POT.` · `THE EXAMPLE DOES THE REAL WORK.` · `NAME THE STEP YOU DISAGREE WITH.` · then, large: `WHERE'S YOUR POT?`

segments.voice: Listen to one sound, a chime if you have one, or whatever comes next, and follow it all the way down into quiet. Then hold up one rule of thumb you live by, like anyone who's late doesn't care, and look for its pot: one real case where it plainly held, and one where it didn't. If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you use as the silence settles.
Nyaya. The school of logic, and its argument in five parts: a claim, a reason, an example you can both see, the fit, and the conclusion.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. A good reason can point to its pot. A week closes on day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students meet Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, learning to set out an argument step by step and to test it in discussion with a teacher.

what a scholar hears: the Nyaya Sutra lists the five members of an argument; Vatsyayana's commentary illustrates them with sound, which is produced, like a pot.

chat.says: Why does Nyaya spell out such obvious steps, like a pot breaking?
options: So the other person can check each step; the pot is a case you've both seen.
It's a memory trick: five short steps are easier to recite than one long one.
Because the longer an argument sounds, the more likely a listener believes it.
chat.meaning: Nyaya says its five parts out loud so another person can test each step, and the example points to a case both have seen, like a pot.
